_sections: After Acts: Mary and the apostles, by tradition
_notes: Lane `tradition` (new): events after or beside Acts that rest on tradition. Each event has `basis`: "Scripture", "Early tradition" or "Later legend", with the sources named in `orderNote`. Routes of Later legend events are drawn dashed (`routeUncertain`).
Explicit `year` on every event; the order is by year, not by any harmony.

zaragoza.name: Caesaraugusta (Zaragoza)
zaragoza.note: A Roman colony on the Ebro, founded under Augustus about 14 BC and named for him; the name wore down to Zaragoza. Spanish tradition places here the Virgin's appearance to St James on a pillar of jasper, now kept in the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar on the river bank.

maryhouse.name: House of the Virgin Mary (Meryemana)
maryhouse.note: A small stone chapel on Mount Koressos (Bülbüldağı), about 4 miles above ancient Ephesus. Lazarist priests from Smyrna identified it in 1891 by following the visions of Anne Catherine Emmerich; the walls rest on foundations perhaps of the 1st century, with a building of the 6th or 7th. It is a place of pilgrimage for Christians and Muslims, who honor Maryam as well.

compostela.name: Santiago de Compostela
compostela.note: A city in the far northwest of Spain, grown up around a Roman-era tomb identified in the early 9th century as that of St James the Greater. The cathedral stands over the tomb, and the Way of St James, the Camino, has drawn pilgrims from across Europe since the Middle Ages.

dormition.name: Dormition Abbey, Mount Zion
dormition.note: Jerusalem tradition, recorded from the 5th century, says Mary lived her last days on Mount Zion near the room of the Last Supper and fell asleep there. The Byzantine church of Hagia Sion stood on the site; the present Benedictine abbey, with its round tower, was finished in 1910.

marystomb.name: Tomb of the Virgin Mary, Kidron Valley
marystomb.note: A rock-cut tomb at the foot of the Mount of Olives, near Gethsemane, honored since at least the 5th century as the place where the apostles laid Mary's body. A Crusader stairway of 47 steps leads down to the tomb chamber, which is shared by Greek Orthodox and Armenian clergy.

muziris.name: Muziris (Kodungallur)
muziris.note: The great pepper port of the Malabar coast, reached by Roman ships riding the monsoon from the Red Sea; Pliny the Elder calls it "the first emporium of India." Its exact site was lost; finds at Pattanam, near Kodungallur in Kerala, since 2007 may mark it. Kerala's Saint Thomas Christians hold that Thomas landed here in AD 52.

patras.name: Patrae (Patras)
patras.note: A Roman colony on the Gulf of Patras in the northwest Peloponnese, refounded by Augustus. The Basilica of St Andrew, finished in 1974, is the largest church in Greece; it keeps the head of St Andrew, returned from St Peter's in Rome in 1964, and pieces of the cross on which he is said to have died.

tarraco.name: Tarraco (Tarragona)
tarraco.note: Capital of the province of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the Mediterranean coast of Catalonia, with an amphitheatre, circus and forum whose ruins survive. Local tradition says Paul preached here on his journey to Spain; the cathedral keeps a chapel in his honor.

quovadis.name: Domine Quo Vadis church, Appian Way
quovadis.note: A small church on the Appian Way, about a mile outside the Porta San Sebastiano, marks where, in the story, Peter met Christ as he fled the city. A copy of a stone with two footprints, said to be Christ's, is kept inside; the original is in the nearby Basilica of St Sebastian.

vatican.name: Vatican Hill (St Peter's)
vatican.note: In Nero's day a district of gardens, a circus and a cemetery across the Tiber. Tradition from the 2nd century places Peter's martyrdom and tomb here; Constantine built the first St Peter's over the tomb about AD 320, and excavations in the 1940s found the shrine of about AD 160 under the high altar.

trefontane.name: Tre Fontane (Aquae Salviae)
trefontane.note: A wooded hollow off the road to Ostia, then called Aquae Salviae, where tradition says Paul was beheaded. Legend adds that his head struck the ground three times and three springs rose; a Trappist abbey and three churches stand there. His tomb is honored about 2 miles away, in St Paul Outside the Walls.

pella.name: Pella (Tabaqat Fahl)
pella.note: A city of the Decapolis on the east slope of the Jordan Valley, in modern Jordan. Ruins of a Roman theatre, Byzantine churches and much older settlements cover the mound and the valley at Tabaqat Fahl.

mylapore.name: Mylapore (Chennai)
mylapore.note: An old quarter of Chennai on the Bay of Bengal. Syriac tradition from the 4th century says Thomas was killed near here and buried at Mylapore; the San Thome Basilica, rebuilt in neo-Gothic style in 1896, stands over the tomb, and St Thomas Mount nearby is honored as the place of his death.

hierapolis.name: Hierapolis (Pamukkale)
hierapolis.note: A spa city above the white travertine terraces of Pamukkale in western Turkey, near Laodicea and Colossae; Paul names its Christians in Colossians 4:13. A 5th-century martyrium of St Philip stands on the hill above the city.

stjohn.name: Basilica of St John, Ayasuluk (Selçuk)
stjohn.note: On Ayasuluk hill above Ephesus, Justinian built a great domed basilica in the 6th century over the grave honored as the Apostle John's. Its ruins, partly restored, stand below the Byzantine and Ottoman citadel in the town of Selçuk.

patmos.name: Patmos
patmos.note: A small rocky island in the Aegean, about 60 miles southwest of Ephesus. The Cave of the Apocalypse, where tradition says John received his visions, lies halfway up the hill to the Monastery of St John the Theologian, founded in 1088; both are a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.

events.title: Mary in the house of John
events.summary: From the cross Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple whom he loved, and from that hour the disciple takes her into his own home. After the Ascension she is with the apostles, the women and Jesus' brethren in the upper room, devoted to prayer as they wait for the Spirit. This is the last time Scripture names her. Everything after rests on tradition, which divides on where she spent her last years: in Jerusalem, or with John at Ephesus.

scripture.text: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.
All these with one accord devoted themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.

events.orderNote: Basis: Scripture. John 19:25–27 and Acts 1:14 are the last New Testament mentions of Mary by name. The "Beyond Acts" lane that follows sets traditions beside Scripture, each marked by how old and how firm its witness is.

art.title: The Crucifixion with the Virgin and St John
art.location: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
art.description: Against a dark night sky with stars, the gaunt Christ hangs on the cross between the grieving Virgin Mary and John, who looks up with open hands.
art.significance: Ter Brugghen, a Dutch follower of Caravaggio, deliberately echoed old German art in this stark altarpiece, probably made for a hidden Catholic church in Utrecht.
art.symbolism: Only Mary and John stand beneath the cross, the two whom Jesus gave to each other from it.
art.impact: Long lost, it resurfaced in England in the 1950s and is now one of the Met's most striking Dutch paintings.

events.title: James in Spain and Our Lady of the Pillar
people: James the Greater, son of Zebedee
events.summary: Spanish tradition says that James, brother of John, carried the gospel to the far west of the empire, to Hispania, and had little success. As he prayed one night by the Ebro at Caesaraugusta, discouraged, the Virgin Mary appeared to him on a pillar of jasper, while she was still living in Jerusalem, and told him to build a church there. He did, and returned to Jerusalem, where Herod Agrippa I had him killed. The pillar is venerated in Zaragoza's basilica, and Spain keeps her feast on 12 October.
events.journey: Unknown. By sea from Joppa the whole length of the Mediterranean to the coast of Hispania, then up the Ebro valley. The route drawn is only a guess at a likely sea lane, and the voyage itself is legend.

scripture.text: He killed James the brother of John with the sword;

events.orderNote: Basis: Later legend. The New Testament says nothing of James leaving Judea, and Paul writes in Romans 15:20–24 as though no apostle had yet preached in Spain. The claim first appears in the Breviarium Apostolorum, a Latin list of the apostles' missions from about AD 600, and the story of the pillar is written down in Zaragoza only in the 13th century; a church of St Mary there is known from the 9th.

events.title: Mary goes with John to Ephesus
events.summary: One tradition holds that when persecution came to Jerusalem, John took Mary with him to Ephesus, where she lived her last years in a small house on the hill above the city. Its modern form rests on the visions of the German mystic Anne Catherine Emmerich (died 1824), from which Lazarist priests found the ruined house at Meryemana in 1891. Popes Paul VI (1967), John Paul II (1979) and Benedict XVI (2006) prayed there, and it draws pilgrims of many faiths.
events.journey: Overland or by sea from Judea to the coast of Asia, perhaps 700 miles. No early source describes the journey; the line is drawn only to show the distance.

scripture.text: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.

events.orderNote: Basis: Later legend, resting on a real but slender early witness. The Council of Ephesus in 431 met in a church of St Mary there, and its letter mentions "John the Theologian and the holy Virgin" at Ephesus, though scholars differ on whether this means she lived or was buried there. No writer before the Middle Ages says plainly that she died at Ephesus; the older Jerusalem tradition places her death on Mount Zion. The site of the house comes from Emmerich's visions, published by Clemens Brentano, and the Church has never ruled on it.

events.title: The body of St James is brought to Compostela
people: His disciples Athanasius and Theodore (in the legend)
Bishop Theodemir of Iria Flavia (9th century)
events.summary: After Herod Agrippa I put James to death in Jerusalem, legend says his disciples carried his body by a boat without sails or rudder to Iria Flavia, on the coast of Galicia, and buried it inland. The tomb was forgotten until about the 820s, when the hermit Pelagius saw lights over a field, and Bishop Theodemir declared the grave to be the apostle's. King Alfonso II built a church; the shrine grew into the cathedral of Santiago, and the Way of St James became one of the great pilgrimages of Christendom.
events.journey: Legend says the boat crossed the whole Mediterranean and rounded Spain in seven days. The line drawn follows the sea route the story implies and is not history.

scripture.text: He killed James the brother of John with the sword;

events.orderNote: Basis: Later legend. Acts 12:2 records James's death in Jerusalem about AD 44 and says nothing of his burial. The finding of the tomb under Bishop Theodemir (died 847) is told in sources of the 11th and 12th centuries, chiefly the Concordia de Antealtares and the Codex Calixtinus. Excavations under the cathedral in 1946–1959 found a Roman-era cemetery and a mausoleum, but nothing that names who lies there.

art.title: The Translation of the Body of St James before the Palace of Queen Lupa
art.description: The apostle's disciples bring his body on an ox cart to the palace of Lupa, a pagan queen of Galicia, who in the legend tried to trick them with wild bulls that turned tame and drew the cart themselves.
art.significance: A panel from a Spanish Gothic altarpiece of the life of St James, painted in Aragon, where the legend of James in Spain was dear.
art.symbolism: The wild oxen tamed under the yoke show the power of the saint even in death, and the conversion of Galicia that the legend tells.
art.impact: Altarpieces like this spread the story of Compostela to the pilgrims who walked the Camino.

events.title: The Dormition: Mary falls asleep
people: The apostles, gathered from far away (in the tradition)
events.summary: The East calls Mary's death her Dormition, her "falling asleep." The tradition says that, knowing her end was near, she prayed in her house on Mount Zion, and the apostles were brought together from the ends of the earth to be with her. Christ himself came to receive her soul, and the apostles carried her body to a new tomb in the valley of Jehoshaphat, the Kidron. The Church does not say how or when she died, and gives no date; the tradition places it some years after the Resurrection.
events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition, though not early history. The story is told in the many "Transitus Mariae" (Passing of Mary) writings, in Syriac, Greek, Latin and other languages, the oldest from the late 5th century and drawing on earlier lost texts. The church of Hagia Sion on Mount Zion was honored as the place by the 6th century. The year shown here is only a placeholder; the tradition gives dates from 3 to 15 years after the Ascension.

art.title: The Death of the Virgin
art.description: Mary lies on a bier in a great hall, surrounded by the apostles holding candles, a censer and a book; through the window a calm view opens over the lagoon and bridge of Mantua.
art.significance: Painted for the chapel of the Gonzaga court at Mantua, it is one of Mantegna's most perfect small works, with a deep, exact perspective.
art.symbolism: The open window and still water carry the eye from the death chamber to a wide world of light, a sign of her passing to glory.
art.impact: Mantegna's balance of grief and calm set a model for later Italian images of the Dormition.

events.title: The Assumption of Mary
people: Thomas, who arrived late (in some versions)
events.summary: The apostles lay Mary's body in a tomb near Gethsemane. In many tellings Thomas comes late, the tomb is opened for him, and it is empty, with only her grave clothes and the scent of flowers. The Church believes that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Pope Pius XII defined this as dogma in 1950, without saying whether she died first; the Assumption is celebrated on 15 August.
events.journey: The burial procession, about half a mile from Mount Zion down into the Kidron Valley.

scripture.text: And a great portent appeared in heaven, a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars;

echoes.note: "Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might": the Fathers read the ark as a figure of Mary, the dwelling of God's presence.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. Scripture does not describe Mary's death or assumption; Revelation 12 is read of her, among other meanings, in the liturgy. The empty tomb appears in the Transitus writings of the 5th century; St John Damascene (8th century) tells that Bishop Juvenal of Jerusalem informed the emperor Marcian about 451 that the tomb was empty. The Emperor Maurice fixed the feast on 15 August about AD 600. Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus, 1 November 1950.

art.title: The Assumption of the Virgin (Assunta)
art.location: Basilica of Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari, Venice
art.description: On a cloud borne by a crowd of child angels, Mary rises with her arms raised toward God the Father, while the apostles below reach up in wonder and alarm.
art.significance: Nearly 23 feet high, it made the young Titian famous and is still in place over the high altar it was painted for.
art.symbolism: Three zones, earth, Mary and heaven, are joined by her movement upward and by the red of her robe and of the apostles' cloaks.
art.impact: Its sweeping energy shaped Baroque altarpieces for two centuries.

events.title: Thomas sails to India
people: Habban, the king's merchant (in the Acts of Thomas)
events.summary: When the apostles cast lots for the nations, the Acts of Thomas says, India fell to Thomas. He did not want to go, so the risen Lord sold him as a slave-carpenter to Habban, a merchant of King Gondophares, and Thomas sailed east and preached in the king's realm. Kerala's Saint Thomas Christians keep their own tradition: that he landed at Muziris (Kodungallur) in AD 52 and founded seven churches along the Malabar coast. The apostle who said "My Lord and my God!" carried that faith farther from Jerusalem than any of the Twelve.
events.journey: Perhaps 3,000 miles: overland to the Red Sea, then on one of the merchant ships that sailed with the summer monsoon from Egypt's Red Sea ports across the Arabian Sea to the Malabar coast, a voyage of about 40 days at sea. The line follows the trade route Pliny describes; the Acts of Thomas gives no route.

scripture.text: Thomas answered him, "My Lord and my God!"

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. The Acts of Thomas, written in Syriac at Edessa in the early 3rd century, tells of his mission to King Gondophares. Gondophares was long thought a fiction, until coins and the Takht-i-Bahi inscription (found 1857, dated to about AD 46) showed an Indo-Parthian king of that name ruling in what is now Pakistan and Afghanistan. Origen, as quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.1), gives Thomas Parthia; Ephrem and later Syriac writers speak of India. The landing at Muziris in AD 52 is the Kerala tradition, written down later but held for centuries.

art.title: Silver tetradrachm of Gondophares
art.description: A coin of King Gondophares, showing the king on horseback on one side and a standing god on the other, with inscriptions in Greek and Kharoshthi.
art.significance: Coins like this proved that Gondophares, the king of the Acts of Thomas, was a real ruler of the 1st century in the borderlands of India.
art.symbolism: The two scripts, Greek and Indian, show a kingdom where the Mediterranean and India met.
art.impact: The discovery gave historical weight to the old tradition of Thomas in India.
art.credit: Photo: Jean-Michel Moullec from Vern sur Seiche (35, Bret, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: Andrew is martyred at Patras
people: Aegeates, the proconsul (in the Acts of Andrew)
Maximilla, his wife, a Christian convert (in the Acts of Andrew)
events.summary: Andrew, the first to follow Jesus and the one who brought his brother Simon to him, is said to have preached around the Black Sea and in Greece. At Patras, the story goes, the proconsul's wife Maximilla became a Christian and left her husband's bed, and he had Andrew crucified. Andrew was bound rather than nailed, so that he would suffer longer, and preached from the cross for days until he died. The X-shaped cross, now the saltire of Scotland, belongs to later medieval art; earlier images show an ordinary cross.

scripture.text: One of the two who heard John speak, and followed him, was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his brother Simon, and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. Origen, as quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.1), says Andrew's lot was Scythia, north of the Black Sea. The Acts of Andrew, from the late 2nd century, sets his martyrdom at Patras; the date of about AD 60 is traditional. His relics were taken to Constantinople in 357, and his head, kept in Rome from 1462, was given back to Patras by Pope Paul VI in 1964.

art.title: The Martyrdom of St Andrew
art.description: Andrew, bound to an X-shaped cross, looks up toward a burst of light where angels descend with a palm and wreath, while soldiers on horseback and onlookers gather below.
art.significance: A late work of the Seville master, painted with the soft, glowing light of his mature style.
art.symbolism: The saltire cross became Andrew's emblem; the light from heaven turns the execution into a welcome.
art.impact: Murillo's gentle, luminous piety made him one of the most loved painters of Spain.

events.title: James, the brother of the Lord, is killed
events.summary: James, "the brother of the Lord," led the church in Jerusalem after Peter left; Paul calls him one of its pillars. In AD 62 the procurator Festus died, and before his successor Albinus arrived, the high priest Ananus called the Sanhedrin, accused James and others of breaking the law, and had them stoned. Fair-minded citizens complained, and Ananus was deposed after three months. A later Christian account has James thrown from the Temple's pinnacle, stoned, and struck down with a fuller's club, praying for his killers.

scripture.text: and when they perceived the grace that was given to me, James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised;

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition, and history. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing about AD 93, records the death of "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James" (Antiquities 20.200). The fuller's club and the fall from the Temple come from Hegesippus, a 2nd-century Christian writer quoted by Eusebius (Church History 2.23). James wrote, by tradition, the Letter of James; Catholics identify him with James son of Alphaeus, the Orthodox keep them distinct.

art.title: St James, Brother of the Lord, Enthroned
art.description: James sits enthroned in bishop's vestments, blessing with one hand and holding an open Gospel book; small images of the Virgin and Child and of Christ appear in the upper corners, and the donor kneels at his feet.
art.significance: Tzanes was a leading Cretan icon painter who worked in Venice; James appears as first bishop of Jerusalem.
art.symbolism: The bishop's omophorion marks him as head of the mother church of Jerusalem; the gold background is the light of heaven.
art.impact: The Liturgy of St James, still used on his feast, keeps his memory in Eastern worship.

events.title: Paul goes on to Spain?
events.summary: Paul had told the Romans he hoped to see them on his way to Spain. If, as early writers believed, he was freed after his two years under guard, he may have made that journey. Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says Paul taught righteousness to the whole world and came "to the limits of the west" before he bore witness. Tarragona, the capital of eastern Spain, claims his preaching. Others think the trial in Rome ended in his death, and the Spanish journey never happened.
events.journey: About 850 miles by sea from Ostia, along the coast of Gaul or straight across to the Spanish coast. A voyage Paul hoped for; whether he made it is not known, so the line is dashed.

scripture.text: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be sped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a little.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition, disputed. 1 Clement 5 (c. AD 96) says Paul reached "the limits of the west," which in Rome likely meant Spain; the Muratorian fragment (late 2nd century) speaks of "Paul's departure from the city on his journey to Spain." The Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) imply travels in the East after Acts. Many scholars doubt any release. The route is drawn dashed for that reason.

events.title: “Lord, where are you going?”
events.summary: When Nero turned on the Christians after the great fire of July AD 64, the Christians of Rome begged Peter to save himself, and he left the city by night. On the road, the story says, he met Christ walking toward Rome and asked him, "Domine, quo vadis?" Lord, where are you going? Christ answered, "I am going to Rome to be crucified again." Peter understood, turned back, and went to his death. The little church on the Appian Way marks the place.
events.journey: About 2 miles out from the city along the Appian Way, and back again.

scripture.text: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterward."

events.orderNote: Basis: Later legend, though old. The meeting is told in the apocryphal Acts of Peter, written about AD 180–190; Ambrose of Milan retells it in the 4th century. The church Domine Quo Vadis was rebuilt in its present form in 1637. The story echoes John 13:36, Peter's question at the Last Supper, and the Lord's answer that he would follow later.

art.title: Domine, Quo Vadis?
art.description: On a road outside Rome, Christ, carrying his cross, strides toward the viewer; Peter starts back in astonishment, his arms thrown out.
art.significance: A small, powerful work from Carracci's Roman years, painted with few figures and strong gestures.
art.symbolism: The cross Christ carries foretells Peter's own; Christ's pointing hand turns him back toward Rome and his martyrdom.
art.impact: It fixed the image of the Quo Vadis story in Western art and was widely copied.

events.title: Peter is crucified in Rome
events.summary: Jesus had told Peter by the lake that when he was old he would stretch out his hands and be led where he did not wish to go. In Nero's persecution, Peter was crucified in Rome, near the emperor's circus on the Vatican Hill, and buried in the cemetery beside it. Origen, the early 3rd-century scholar, says he asked to be crucified head down, not thinking himself worthy to die as his Lord had. Christians remembered the place: a small shrine of about AD 160 marked it, Constantine built a basilica over it, and St Peter's stands there still.
events.journey: Back through the city and across the Tiber to the Vatican, about 4 miles.

scripture.text: Truly, truly, I say to you, when you were young, you girded yourself and walked where you would; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish to go." (This he said to show by what death he was to glorify God.)
She who is at Babylon, who is likewise chosen, sends you greetings; and so does my son Mark.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition, and well attested. 1 Clement 5–6 (c. AD 96) joins Peter's and Paul's martyrdoms to Nero's persecution; Tacitus (Annals 15.44) describes the persecution itself. Tertullian (c. 200) says Peter suffered "a passion like his Lord's" in Rome, and Origen (in Eusebius, Church History 3.1) that he was crucified head downward. About 200 the Roman priest Gaius pointed to the "trophies" of the apostles on the Vatican and the Ostian Way. Excavations under St Peter's in 1939–1949 found that shrine, and Pope Paul VI announced in 1968 that bones from it had been identified, with moral certainty, as Peter's.

art.title: The Crucifixion of St Peter
art.location: Cerasi Chapel, Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome
art.description: Three laborers strain to raise the heavy cross on which Peter is nailed head down; the old apostle lifts his head and looks past the nails.
art.significance: Painted for the same chapel as Carracci's altarpiece; Caravaggio shows the event as hard, physical work, with the executioners' faces hidden.
art.symbolism: The upside-down cross, Peter's chosen humility, is now itself a symbol of the papacy.
art.impact: Its realism and raking light made it one of the defining images of Baroque Rome.

events.title: Paul is beheaded on the Ostian Way
events.summary: In 2 Timothy Paul writes from a second, harsher imprisonment: only Luke is with him, he has fought the good fight, and the time of his departure has come. As a Roman citizen he could not be crucified, and tradition says he was beheaded with the sword outside the city, at Aquae Salviae on the road to Ostia, and buried by the road nearby. Over the grave Constantine built a church, rebuilt on a grand scale as St Paul Outside the Walls.
events.journey: Out of the city by the Ostian Gate and south along the Via Laurentina, about 3 miles.

scripture.text: For I am already on the point of being sacrificed; the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. 1 Clement 5 (c. AD 96) says Paul "bore witness before the rulers" after reaching the limits of the west. Eusebius (Church History 2.25) says he was beheaded in Rome under Nero, and quotes Gaius on his "trophy" on the Ostian Way. Tre Fontane is named as the place of death from the 6th century. A marble sarcophagus under the high altar of St Paul Outside the Walls was examined in 2006–2009; bone fragments inside were dated to the 1st or 2nd century.

art.title: The Beheading of St Paul
art.description: Paul's body lies on the ground after the sword stroke, his haloed head beside it, while Roman soldiers and a crowd in pale robes press around in a hazy street.
art.significance: Simonet painted it as a scholarship student in Rome and showed it in Madrid in 1887, where it was much admired.
art.symbolism: The light around the fallen head marks him a saint at the moment of death; the sword, the instrument of his martyrdom, is his emblem in art.
art.impact: It made Simonet's name and became one of the best-known Spanish religious paintings of the 19th century.

events.title: The church of Jerusalem flees to Pella
people: Simeon son of Clopas, James's successor
events.summary: When the Jews of Judea rose against Rome in AD 66, and Roman armies began to close in on Jerusalem, the Christians of the city remembered the Lord's warning to flee to the mountains when they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Warned, it is said, by a revelation, they left before the siege and crossed the Jordan to Pella, a Gentile city of the Decapolis. Titus took Jerusalem and burned the Temple in AD 70; some of the church later returned, under Simeon, a cousin of the Lord.
events.journey: About 60 miles: down to Jericho, north up the Jordan Valley, and across the river to Pella on the eastern slopes.

scripture.text: "But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it;

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. Eusebius (Church History 3.5) says the Jerusalem church was told by an oracle to leave for Pella before the war; Epiphanius (4th century) repeats it. Some scholars doubt it, since both write late, but Pella's Christian community is well attested afterward. Simeon son of Clopas led the church until his martyrdom under Trajan (Eusebius 3.32).

events.title: Thomas is martyred near Mylapore
people: The Christians of the Coromandel coast
events.summary: After years in the south of India, tradition says, Thomas crossed to the eastern, Coromandel coast and was killed with a lance near Mylapore in AD 72, at a hill now called St Thomas Mount. He was buried at Mylapore. Part of his relics were taken to Edessa in Syria by the 4th century and later to Ortona in Italy; the San Thome Basilica in Chennai stands over the original tomb. Thomas, who once said "Let us also go, that we may die with him," kept his word.
events.journey: About 350 miles across the south of India, through the Palghat Gap, from the Malabar coast to the Coromandel coast.

scripture.text: Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. The Acts of Thomas (3rd century) tells of his martyrdom by spear at the order of a king called Mazdai. St Ephrem the Syrian (died 373) writes of his relics brought from India to Edessa. The site at Mylapore was described by travelers from the 13th century, including Marco Polo; the Portuguese rebuilt the church over the tomb in 1523.

art.title: The Martyrdom of St Thomas
art.description: Thomas kneels at a pagan altar as his killers stab him with spears, while angels descend with a wreath and palm.
art.significance: Painted late in Rubens's life for the high altar of the Augustinian church of St Thomas in Prague's Lesser Town; the original is now in the National Gallery Prague.
art.symbolism: The palm and wreath are the martyr's victory; the idol behind shows the faith he would not deny.
art.impact: An example of the grand Counter-Reformation altarpiece that Rubens perfected.

events.title: Philip at Hierapolis
events.summary: Philip of Bethsaida, who brought Nathanael to Jesus, is said to have preached in Phrygia and died at Hierapolis. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus about AD 190, names him among the great lights of Asia and says he "sleeps at Hierapolis" with two of his daughters. Later accounts say he was martyred there under Domitian. In 2011 Italian archaeologists announced they had found a 1st-century tomb, inside a 5th-century church beside the martyrium, which they believe was honored as Philip's.

scripture.text: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. And he found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael, and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
On the morrow we departed and came to Caesarea; and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. And he had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. Polycrates' letter is quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.31 and 5.24). Early writers may have confused the apostle Philip with Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven, whose four prophesying daughters appear in Acts 21:8–9; Eusebius himself treats them as one. The date of about AD 80 is a placeholder; the tradition gives none firmly.

art.title: The Crucifixion of St Philip
art.location: Strozzi Chapel, Santa Maria Novella, Florence
art.description: Philip is hoisted on a cross with ropes and poles by straining workmen, before a crowd and an ornate classical setting.
art.significance: Part of Filippino's fresco cycle for the banker Filippo Strozzi, whose patron saint Philip was; a companion scene shows Philip driving a dragon from the temple at Hierapolis.
art.symbolism: The fantastic antique architecture evokes the pagan city whose idols Philip defied.
art.impact: The Strozzi Chapel frescoes are among the most inventive of late 15th-century Florence.

events.title: John's last years at Ephesus
events.summary: The last of the apostles to die, tradition says, John lived to a great age at Ephesus, leading the churches of Asia, and there wrote or gave his Gospel. Irenaeus, who knew Polycarp, says John stayed in Ephesus until the time of Trajan. Jerome tells that, too old to preach, he was carried into the assembly and said only, "Little children, love one another," and when asked why always the same words, answered that it was the Lord's command and enough. He was buried on the hill of Ayasuluk.

scripture.text: This is the disciple who is bearing witness to these things, and who has written these things; and we know that his testimony is true.

events.orderNote: Basis: Early tradition. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.1.1 and 3.3.4, c. 180) says John published his Gospel at Ephesus and lived there until Trajan (98–117). Polycrates of Ephesus (c. 190) says John "sleeps at Ephesus." The "little children" saying is in Jerome's commentary on Galatians (6.10). Some scholars think the John of Ephesus was a different John, "the elder," mentioned by Papias. Justinian's basilica over the tomb dates from the 6th century.

events.title: John on Patmos: the Revelation
events.summary: John writes that he was on the island called Patmos "on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus," exiled, it seems, for his preaching. On the Lord's day he was in the Spirit and heard a loud voice telling him to write what he saw and send it to the seven churches of Asia: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea. The book that follows, the Revelation, ends the Bible with the vision of a new heaven and a new earth. Tradition says he was freed after Domitian's death in AD 96 and returned to Ephesus.
events.journey: Down the Cayster to the coast and about 60 miles by sea, southwest past Samos to Patmos.

scripture.text: I John, your brother, who share with you in Jesus the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance, was on the island called Patmos on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.

events.orderNote: Basis: Scripture for John's stay on Patmos (Revelation 1:9). The date comes from Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3), who says the vision was seen "toward the end of Domitian's reign" (81–96); Eusebius (3.18 and 3.20) adds the exile and return. Whether the John of Revelation is the apostle has been debated since the 3rd century; the Church's tradition holds that he is.

art.title: St John the Evangelist on the Island of Patmos
art.description: A young John sits with pen and book, looking up at the vision of the woman clothed with the sun, with an eagle at his side.
art.significance: One of Velázquez's earliest religious works, painted in Seville at about nineteen for a Carmelite convent.
art.symbolism: The eagle is John's emblem; the vision in the sky is the woman of Revelation 12, read as Mary.
art.impact: It was paired with his Immaculate Conception, linking John's vision to Spain's devotion to Mary.
